body:
A lawn fertilizer calculator turns the three numbers on a bag into pounds you can spread: product needed = nitrogen rate divided by the bag nitrogen share, times your lawn area divided by 1,000. For a common 24-0-6 lawn food at the standard 1 lb nitrogen rate, that is 4.17 lb of product per 1,000 sq ft. Most home lawns need 15 to 45 lb of product per feeding, so most owners buy one or two bags at a time. This guide shows the math, a full worked example, and how to set a spreader so the bag matches the plan.

## The fertilizer formula in plain words

The first number on the bag is the nitrogen share by weight. A 24-0-6 bag is 24 percent nitrogen, 0 percent phosphate, and 6 percent potash. Only the nitrogen number drives this math, because lawn feeding rates are set in pounds of actual nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft.

**Pounds of product per 1,000 sq ft = target lb of nitrogen / (bag nitrogen percent / 100).**

**Total product = pounds per 1,000 sq ft x lawn area / 1,000.**

**Bags = total product / bag weight, rounded up.**

| Bag analysis | Nitrogen share | Product per 1,000 sq ft at 1 lb N rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10-10-10 | 10 percent | 10.00 lb |
| 16-4-8 | 16 percent | 6.25 lb |
| 24-0-6 | 24 percent | 4.17 lb |
| 32-0-10 | 32 percent | 3.13 lb |

The table is the same formula at four bag strengths. Weak bags take more pounds to deliver the same nitrogen, so compare cost per pound of nitrogen, not cost per bag. A soil test from your state extension lab tells you if you need the middle and last numbers at all. Many lawns need nitrogen only, and extra phosphorus just washes away.

Extension services set the rate, not the bag cover. Cornell's turf program says never apply more than 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per application. Kansas State and the University of New Hampshire give the same 1 lb cap in their home lawn guides. Keep clippings on the lawn and Cornell notes the need for nitrogen can drop by 25 to 50 percent.

## Worked example: a 6,000 sq ft lawn with 24-0-6

Say your lawn measures 6,000 sq ft (557 sq m) after you subtract the house, driveway, and beds. You picked a 24-0-6 fertilizer in a 15 lb bag, and your target is 1.0 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft for a fall feeding.

Step 1, product per 1,000 sq ft: 1.0 / 0.24 = 4.17 lb of product.

Step 2, scale to the lawn: 4.17 x (6,000 / 1,000) = 4.17 x 6 = 25.0 lb of product.

Step 3, bags: 25.0 / 15 = 1.67 bags. You cannot spread part of a plan, so round up and buy 2 bags. You will use about 25 lb and keep about 5 lb dry in the bag for a small spring touch-up, or buy one 15 lb bag and one smaller bag if the store stocks one.

Check the math a second way, by nitrogen. Total nitrogen needed is 6 x 1.0 = 6 lb. One 15 lb bag at 24 percent holds 15 x 0.24 = 3.6 lb of nitrogen. Bags needed: 6 / 3.6 = 1.67 bags, the same answer. Round up to 2 bags, set the spreader for about 4.2 lb per 1,000 sq ft, and weigh what is left after the first pass if you want a tight check.

## How to measure your lawn area

Measure lawn only, not the whole lot. Pace or tape the front, side, and back lawns as rectangles, multiply length x width for each, and add them. Subtract the house, driveway, patio, and big beds. A 60 x 100 ft lot is 6,000 sq ft on paper, but the true lawn is often 3,500 to 4,500 sq ft once the hard parts come out.

For an odd lot, split it into rectangles and one triangle if needed. Triangle area is base x height / 2. Our [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) handles those shapes, and our [mulch calculator](/blog/mulch-calculator/) covers the beds you subtracted. Write the final lawn area on the garage wall.

## Set the spreader so the math survives the lawn

A calculator gives pounds. A spreader gives a dial number, and the two only meet if you check the output. Use the bag's printed setting for your spreader model as a start, set it a notch lower, and spread a test strip over a tarp of known size. Weigh the product caught, compare it with the target per 1,000 sq ft, and adjust the dial.

Walk at a steady pace in straight lines, with slight overlap at the edges, and shut the hopper at each turn. Sweep or blow granules off the driveway and sidewalk back onto the grass. Product left on concrete washes into storm drains, and extension guides flag that as the easiest waste to prevent.

Water lightly after a granular feeding if no rain is due within a day. Do not feed before a heavy storm, onto frozen ground, or in summer heat. On cool-season lawns, the fall feeding does the most good, and mid-summer feeding is the one to skip in most years.

## Mistakes that burn grass or waste money

The classic error is reading the bag weight as nitrogen weight. A 15 lb bag of 24-0-6 holds 3.6 lb of nitrogen, not 15 lb, and owners who miss that point under-feed by a wide mark. The reverse error is worse: doubling the rate to make the lawn extra green. Past 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft in one pass, you risk salt burn, brown tips, and fast soft growth that disease loves.

Skipping the soil test is a slower waste. Lawns fed 10-10-10 for years can carry high phosphorus while still needing nitrogen. One test every two or three years fixes the plan. Keep bags dry and sealed, because damp fertilizer clumps and dumps in piles that scorch the grass.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much fertilizer do I need for 5,000 sq ft?
At 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft with a 24-0-6 bag, you need 4.17 x 5 = 20.8 lb of product. That is two 15 lb bags bought, with about 9 lb left over, or one larger bag if the store stocks a 25 lb size. With a 10-10-10 bag you need 10 x 5 = 50 lb.

### What does 24-0-6 mean on a fertilizer bag?
The numbers are percent by weight of nitrogen, phosphate, and potash, in that order. A 15 lb bag of 24-0-6 holds 15 x 0.24 = 3.6 lb of nitrogen, no phosphate, and 15 x 0.06 = 0.9 lb of potash. The rest is carrier and filler that helps you spread it evenly.

### How often should I fertilize my lawn?
Most cool-season lawns do well on one fall feeding, and better lawns get a second in spring, each at up to 1 lb of nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft. Cornell puts good lawns at 0 to 1 applications a year and top lawns at 3 to 4 lighter ones. Your soil test and grass type set the final count.

### Can I put down too much fertilizer at once?
Yes. Past 1 lb of actual nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft in one pass, burn risk climbs fast, and runoff waste climbs with it. Split a heavy plan into two half passes a few weeks apart. If you over-apply by accident, water the area well to move product into the soil.

### Should I fertilize before or after rain?
Feed before a light rain if you can, since the rain waters granules in for free. Skip feeding before a heavy storm, because fast runoff carries product off the lawn and into drains. With no rain due, run the sprinkler for a short cycle after spreading.

## Next step
Measure your lawn once, note the area, and run your bag numbers in the calculator at the top of this page before you shop. Use the same area for the beds you skipped with our [mulch calculator](/blog/mulch-calculator/) and you have the whole yard on one list.
